steps.eyebrow: Plotting directly from pandas DataFrames with seaborn
steps.title: seaborn's DataFrame-first interface
steps.lede: seaborn functions take a DataFrame and column names—no array extraction needed.

blocks.text: Most matplotlib calls require you to extract a column from orders yourself before plotting it. Seaborn's plotting functions operate on DataFrames and arrays containing whole datasets, taking only the names of the variables and their roles in the plot—data=, x=, y=—rather than requiring the caller to extract each array.

sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes') plots average delivery time per city directly from the orders DataFrame and its column names—no separate .groupby() call needed first. Its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar automatically.

opt_correct.message: Correct. Seaborn takes the DataFrame via `data=` and column names via `x=` and `y=`, then computes the mean per category automatically — no `.groupby()` needed.

opt_groupby.message: Seaborn does not need a `.groupby()` call first. Pass the full DataFrame to `data=` and the column names to `x=` and `y=` — seaborn computes the mean per category automatically.

opt_arrays.message: Passing `orders['delivery_time_minutes'].mean()` gives a single scalar, not per-city means. Pass the full DataFrame to `data=` and the column name string to `y=` — seaborn handles the aggregation.

opt_plt.message: `plt.bar()` is a matplotlib function that requires pre-aggregated data. Seaborn's `sns.barplot()` accepts the raw DataFrame and computes the mean per category automatically.

correct.message: Right. Seaborn's `data=`, `x=`, `y=` interface lets you pass the DataFrame and column names directly — it handles the aggregation for you.

incorrect.message: Use `sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes')`. Seaborn takes the full DataFrame and column name strings, then computes the mean per category automatically.

hints: Seaborn's plotting functions take `data=` (the DataFrame) and `x=`/`y=` (column name strings), not extracted arrays.

steps.title: Automatic statistical estimation
steps.lede: Some seaborn functions compute statistics—means, regression lines—automatically.

blocks.text: Many seaborn functions automatically perform the statistical estimation necessary to answer questions such as the average value of one variable as a function of other variables. The sns.barplot() call from before is one such example—it computed each city's mean delivery time automatically, without a separate .groupby() step.

sns.regplot(data=orders, x='distance_km', y='delivery_time_minutes') plots a scatterplot of the observations together with a fitted linear regression line. It shows the distance/delivery-time scatter with a fitted trend line drawn through it in the same call—no separate fitting step required.

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.show()
# Scatter + fitted regression line in one call

public.prompt: Which statement best describes what seaborn does when you call `sns.barplot(data=orders, x='city', y='delivery_time_minutes')`?

options.text: Seaborn automatically computes the mean delivery time per city and draws a bar for each, without a separate aggregation step.
Seaborn draws one bar per row in the DataFrame, using the raw `delivery_time_minutes` value as the bar height.
Seaborn requires you to compute the mean per city with `.groupby()` before calling `sns.barplot()`.
Seaborn automatically computes the sum of delivery times per city and draws a bar for each.

opt_correct.message: Correct. Many seaborn functions automatically perform the statistical estimation necessary to answer questions such as the average value of one variable as a function of other variables.

opt_raw.message: Seaborn does not draw one bar per row. It aggregates the data — by default computing the mean per category — and draws one bar per category.

opt_manual.message: Seaborn does not require a `.groupby()` call. It performs the statistical estimation (mean per category) automatically when you pass the full DataFrame and column names.

opt_sum.message: Seaborn's default estimator is the mean, not the sum. It computes the mean delivery time per city and draws one bar per city.

correct.message: Right. Seaborn automatically performs statistical estimation — `sns.barplot()` computes the mean per category without any manual aggregation.

incorrect.message: Seaborn automatically performs the statistical estimation (mean per category by default) when you pass the full DataFrame and column names — no `.groupby()` needed.

hints: Think about what 'automatic statistical estimation' means — seaborn does the aggregation for you.
The default estimator in `sns.barplot()` is the mean, not the sum or raw values.

public.prompt: An analyst wants to visualize whether longer delivery distances tend to produce longer delivery times, with a fitted trend line drawn through the scatter points. Which seaborn call is correct?

opt_regplot.message: Correct. `sns.regplot(data=..., x=..., y=...)` plots a scatterplot of the observations together with a fitted linear regression line — exactly what is needed to visualize the trend.

opt_barplot.message: `sns.barplot()` computes the mean per category and draws bars. `distance_km` is a continuous numeric variable, not a category — use `sns.regplot()` to show the scatter and fitted trend line.

opt_scatter.message: `plt.scatter()` shows the data points but does not add a fitted trend line. To get both the scatter and the regression line in one call, use `sns.regplot()`.

opt_lineplot.message: `sns.lineplot()` connects data points with a line in the order they appear. It does not fit a regression line. Use `sns.regplot()` to get a scatter plot with a fitted linear regression line.

correct.message: Right. `sns.regplot()` produces a scatterplot with a fitted linear regression line in a single call.

incorrect.message: `sns.regplot(data=orders, x='distance_km', y='delivery_time_minutes')` plots the scatter points and fits a linear regression line through them automatically.

hints: The question asks for a scatter plot with a fitted trend line — which seaborn function adds both in one call?
`sns.regplot()` stands for 'regression plot' — it adds the fitted line automatically.

steps.eyebrow: seaborn built-in themes and color palettes
steps.title: Polishing plots with sns.set_theme()
steps.lede: sns.set_theme() changes the global defaults for all plots—seaborn and matplotlib alike.

blocks.text: sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep') switches to a white background with gridlines and seaborn's 'deep' color palette. The style parameter (default 'darkgrid') controls the background and gridlines; the palette parameter (default 'deep') controls the color sequence.

sns.set_theme() changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn. Because it works by changing global defaults, calling sns.set_theme() changes how plots drawn after that call look—it does not restyle a figure already displayed.

before.title: Default matplotlib style
before.alt_text: Bar chart of category vs value using ds.theming_demo with matplotlib's default white background, blue bars, and no gridlines.

after.code:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep')
sns.barplot(data=theming_demo, x='category', y='value')
plt.show()
# White background, gridlines, seaborn 'deep' palette

annotations.text: set_theme applies style and palette globally via rcParams

public.prompt: A notebook cell calls `sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep')` and then draws a seaborn bar chart. The next cell draws a plain matplotlib line chart without calling `sns.set_theme()` again. What will the matplotlib line chart look like?

options.text: It will use the whitegrid style and deep palette, because `sns.set_theme()` changes global matplotlib rcParams that affect all subsequent plots.
It will use default matplotlib styling, because `sns.set_theme()` only affects seaborn plots.
It will raise an error, because `sns.set_theme()` must be called before every plot.
The seaborn bar chart will be restyled to match the matplotlib defaults.

opt_correct.message: Correct. `sns.set_theme()` changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn.

opt_default.message: `sns.set_theme()` does not only affect seaborn plots. It changes the global matplotlib rcParams, so all subsequent plots — including plain matplotlib ones — use the new style.

opt_error.message: `sns.set_theme()` does not need to be called before every plot. Once called, it changes the global rcParams, which persist for all subsequent plots in the session.

opt_retroactive.message: `sns.set_theme()` changes defaults for plots drawn after the call — it does not go back and restyle a figure you already drew and displayed earlier.

correct.message: Right. `sns.set_theme()` works by changing matplotlib's global rcParams, so it affects every plot drawn after the call — seaborn or not.

incorrect.message: `sns.set_theme()` changes the global matplotlib rcParams. Because it changes global defaults, all plots drawn after the call — including plain matplotlib plots — use the new style.

hints: Think about what 'global defaults' means — once changed, they apply to everything drawn afterward.
`sns.set_theme()` works through matplotlib's rcParams system, not a seaborn-only mechanism.
